explanation: Simple Past regular: verb + -ed. "play -> played", "walk -> walked", "jump -> jumped". If verb ends in -e: just add -d (love -> loved).
options: Add -s (he plays -> he plays)
Add -ing (she walks -> she walking)
Add -ed (play -> played, walk -> walked)
Add -es (go -> goes)
question: How do you form the Simple Past of regular verbs?

explanation: "Go" is irregular: go -> went -> gone. "I went to school yesterday." (Simple Past) vs. "I have gone" (Present Perfect).
options: goed
went
gone
goes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "go"?

explanation: "Write" is irregular: write -> wrote -> written. "She wrote a letter yesterday." (Simple Past) vs. "She has written..." (Present Perfect).
options: writed
wrote
written
wrotes
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "write"?

explanation: "Take" is irregular: take -> took -> taken. "He took the book yesterday." (Simple Past).
options: taked
tooken
took
taken
question: Which is the correct Simple Past of "take"?

explanation: Present Progressive: am/is/are + Verb + -ing. "I am reading." "She is watching TV." "They are playing." Used for: actions happening now, temporary situations.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (I will read)
Subject + have + past participle (I have read)
Subject + am/is/are + verb + -ing (I am reading)
Subject + verb + -s (She reads)
question: How do you form the Present Progressive (Verlaufsform)?

explanation: Present Progressive: 1) now: "I am eating." 2) temporary: "She is living in London for a year." 3) near future plans: "We are meeting tomorrow."
options: For permanent facts and general truths (Water freezes at 0 degrees)
For actions happening right now or around now (I am studying for my exam this week)
For past events that were completed at a specific time
For future plans that are uncertain or impossible to achieve
question: When do we use the Present Progressive?

explanation: Simple Present: habits (I usually get up at 7). Facts (The earth orbits the sun). Progressive: now (She is calling you) or temporary (He is working in Paris this month).
options: There is no real difference - both tenses can always be used interchangeably
Simple Present: habits/facts (I play tennis every week). Progressive: now/temporary (I am playing tennis right now).
Simple Present is more polite and therefore preferred in formal conversations
Progressive is used in writing only; Simple Present is used in speaking
question: What is the difference between Simple Present and Present Progressive?

explanation: Simple Past question: Did + subject + infinitive (no -ed!). "Did you go to school?" "Did she write the letter?" Do NOT say: "Did you went?"
options: Verb + subject + ? (Went you to school?)
Did + subject + infinitive? (Did you see the film?)
Have + subject + past participle? (Have you gone there?)
Will + subject + infinitive? (Will you go there?)
question: How do you form a question in Simple Past?

explanation: Simple Past negative: didn't + infinitive (NOT past tense). "I didn't see him." (NOT: "I didn't saw him") "She didn't go." (NOT: "She didn't went")
options: Subject + no + past tense verb (I no saw him)
Subject + didn't + infinitive (I didn't see him)
Subject + not + past tense verb (I not saw him)
Subject + wasn't + infinitive (I wasn't see him)
question: How do you form a negative in Simple Past?

explanation: Present Perfect (have/has + Partizip II): 1) Erfahrungen: "I have been to Paris." 2) Ergebnis der Vergangenheit relevant jetzt: "She has lost her key." 3) Mit yet, already, just, ever, never.
options: Only for past actions completed at a specific named time (last Tuesday, in 1990)
For experiences, actions with present relevance, or recently completed actions (I have seen this film / She has just arrived)
Only for expressing future events that are planned or scheduled
For describing current habits that happen regularly in the present
question: What is the Present Perfect used for?

explanation: Present Perfect: have/has + Partizip II (3. Form). "I have eaten." "She has gone." "They have played." Regular past participle: verb + -ed. Irregular: go/went/gone, see/saw/seen.
options: Subject + will + infinitive (She will go)
Subject + have/has + past participle (3rd form) (I have eaten / She has gone)
Subject + am/is/are + -ing (She is going)
Subject + did + infinitive (She did go)
question: How do you form the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Used to" + infinitive: frueherer Zustand/Gewohnheit, die jetzt nicht mehr gilt. "I used to eat meat but now I am vegetarian." Nur in der Vergangenheit!
options: A future habit or plan that will be repeated regularly from now on
A past habit or state that no longer exists (I used to play piano - but I don't any more)
A present habit that happens regularly and has not changed
A polite command or request directed at someone else
question: What does "used to" express?

explanation: Comparatives: zwei Dinge vergleichen. Short adjectives: -er. "tall -> taller". Long adjectives: more. "beautiful -> more beautiful". "than" = als.
options: To express that something is the best or highest in a group (the superlative)
To compare two things (She is taller than her brother)
To describe a noun more precisely and add detail to it
To form questions about qualities and characteristics
question: What are comparative adjectives used for?

explanation: "Good" is irregular: good -> better -> best. "This book is better than that one." Common irregular: good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, many/more/most, little/less/least.
options: gooder
more good
better
goodest
question: How do you form the comparative of "good"?

explanation: Long adjectives (3+ syllables): most + adjective. "most interesting". Short adjectives: -est. "big -> biggest". "beautiful -> most beautiful".
options: interestinger
most interesting
interestingest
more interesting
question: How do you form the superlative of "interesting"?

explanation: "Going to" future: am/is/are + going to + infinitive. "I am going to visit Paris next year." Used for plans and intentions, or when evidence shows something will happen.
options: Subject + going to + past tense verb (I going to walked)
Subject + am/is/are + going to + infinitive (I am going to visit Paris)
Subject + will + going + infinitive (I will going visit)
Subject + to + going + infinitive (I to going visit)
question: How do you express the future with "going to"?

explanation: "I will help you!" (spontane Entscheidung). "I am going to visit Rome next summer." (Plan steht schon fest). Both are future but with different nuances.
options: There is no difference - both can always be used interchangeably without change in meaning
Will: spontaneous decisions / predictions. Going to: plans already made / evidence-based predictions.
Will is more formal and therefore preferred in written academic English
Going to describes past plans; will describes current and future intentions
question: What is the difference between "will" and "going to"?

explanation: Conditional I (reale Bedingung): If + Simple Present, will + infinitive. "If the weather is nice, we will go swimming." Reale/moeglich Bedingung.
options: If + past tense, would + infinitive (If it rained, I would stay inside)
If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If it rains, I will stay inside)
If + Past Perfect, would have + past participle (If it had rained, I would have stayed)
If + Present Progressive, am/is/are + going to + infinitive
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 1 (real condition)?

explanation: Conditional II (irreale Bedingung): If + Simple Past, would + infinitive. "If I were rich, I would help everyone." Irreale/unwahrscheinliche Bedingung.
options: If + Simple Present, will + infinitive (If I have money, I will travel)
If + Simple Past, would + infinitive (If I had a million euros, I would travel the world)
If + Present Perfect, would have + past participle (If I have saved, I would travel)
If + Future, will + infinitive (If I will have money, I will travel)
question: How do you form conditional sentences type 2 (unreal condition)?

explanation: Relative clause: "The girl who lives next door is my friend." who = fuer Personen, which = fuer Dinge, that = fuer beides. where = Ort, when = Zeit.
options: A time clause that describes when something happened (when I was young)
A clause that gives more information about a noun, using who/which/that/where/when (The book that I read was exciting)
A conditional clause that describes an imaginary or unlikely situation
A purpose clause that explains why someone did something (so that she could win)
question: What is a relative clause?

explanation: "Who" = fuer Personen. "The man who called is my uncle." "The girl who wrote the letter." Compare: which/that = fuer Sachen.
options: For things and objects (The book who I read was interesting)
For people (The teacher who taught us was strict)
For places (The city who I visited was beautiful)
For times (The day who we met was sunny)
question: When do we use "who" in a relative clause?

explanation: Passive voice: "The letter was written by her." Passive: am/is/are/was/were + past participle. Aktiv betont den Handlungsstaeger, Passiv betont das Ergebnis.
options: She wrote the letter.
The letter was written by her.
She is writing the letter.
She had written the letter.
question: Which sentence uses the passive voice?

explanation: Simple Present Passive: am/is/are + past participle. "English is spoken here." "Milk is sold in shops." "Books are printed in factories."
options: Subject + have been + past participle (have been built)
Subject + is/are + being + past participle (is being built)
Subject + am/is/are + past participle (is built, are sold)
Subject + gets + infinitive (gets build)
question: How do you form the passive in Simple Present?

explanation: Modal verbs: can (koennen), could (koennte), must (muss), should (sollte), may (darf), might (koennte), will (wird), would (wuerde). Modals have no -s in 3rd person and are followed by infinitive.
options: Regular verbs that follow normal conjugation rules (play -> plays -> played)
Auxiliary verbs expressing ability, permission, obligation etc. (can, could, must, should, may, might, will, would)
Irregular verbs whose past tense forms must be memorised individually
Verbs that always end in -ing and describe ongoing or temporary actions
question: What are modal verbs?

explanation: "Must" = interne Notwendigkeit/Regel. "I must study" (ich fuehle die Pflicht). "Have to" = externe Notwendigkeit. "I have to wear a uniform" (Schule schreibt es vor). Often interchangeable.
options: Must and have to always mean completely different things and can never be used the same way
Must: personal obligation/rule. Have to: external obligation. Often similar meaning but must feels more internal.
Must is the past tense form of have to, used to describe past obligations
Have to is always more polite and formal than must in all situations
question: How do you express obligation with "must" vs "have to"?

explanation: "Should" = sollte, Empfehlung. "You should see a doctor." "He shouldn't eat so much sugar." Weaker than must. Used for advice.
options: Certainty - something will definitely happen without any doubt
Advice or recommendation (You should eat more vegetables)
Obligation - a strict rule that must be followed without exception
Permission - asking for or giving someone the right to do something
question: What does "should" express?

explanation: Questions: 1) with auxiliaries (be, have, can): invert subject and auxiliary. "Is she happy?" 2) Simple Present/Past: do/does/did + subject + infinitive. "Do you know her?"
options: Simply add a question mark at the end of any statement without changing word order
Use do/does/did or an auxiliary verb before the subject (Do you like pizza? / Can she swim? / Did he go?)
Put the main verb at the very end of the sentence, as in German word order
Always start the question with the subject, then the verb (You like pizza?)
question: How do you form questions in English?

explanation: Tag questions: am Satzende angefuegt. Positive statement -> negative tag. "It's cold, isn't it?" Negative statement -> positive tag. "You don't know, do you?"
options: Very long and detailed questions that ask for a lot of information at once
Short questions added at the end of a statement to confirm (It's nice, isn't it? / You can swim, can't you?)
Questions that begin with why, asking for the reason behind something
Questions that begin with how, asking about the way or manner of doing something
question: What are tag questions?

explanation: "Neither...nor" = weder...noch. Negative alternative. "I have neither a pen nor a pencil." Compare: "either...or" = entweder...oder.
options: An alternative choice - one of two options that are both possible
Eine doppelte Verneinung - weder...noch (Neither cats nor dogs are allowed here)
Both possibilities - that two things are equally likely or available
A limitation or restriction - that only one thing is allowed or possible
question: What does "neither...nor" express?

explanation: Reported speech: "He said he was tired." (Direct: "I am tired.") Tense shifts back: am -> was, will -> would, can -> could. "that" verbindet.
options: Direct speech - quoting exactly what someone said using quotation marks
Indirect speech - reporting what someone said without quoting exactly (He said that he was tired)
A question that asks someone to repeat or clarify what they just said
A command in which you tell someone to do or not do something directly
question: What is reported speech?

explanation: "I agree with you." Correct. NOT "I am agree" (agree is NOT used with progressive form). State verbs: agree, know, understand, believe, like, love -> no progressive.
options: I am agree with you
I agree with you
I am agreeing with you
I do agree with you (in most contexts)
question: Which sentence is correct?

explanation: State verbs: beschreiben Zustaende, nicht Handlungen. NICHT im Progressive: "I know" (NOT "I am knowing"). "I like" (NOT "I am liking"). "She owns a car" (NOT "she is owning").
options: Action verbs that describe physical movement or activity (run, jump, swim, dance)
Verbs that describe a state, not an action - NOT used in progressive (know, believe, like, love, own, understand)
Irregular verbs whose past tense and past participle must be memorised
Modal verbs that express ability, permission, or obligation (can, must, should)
question: What are "stative verbs" (Zustandsverben)?

explanation: "As well as" = sowohl...als auch / sowie. "She can sing as well as dance." "He likes history as well as geography." Adds information.
options: aber / however - introducing a contrast or contradiction to what was just said
sowie/ebenfalls - adding additional information (She plays piano as well as guitar)
weder...noch - saying that two things are both not the case or not allowed
entweder...oder - presenting two mutually exclusive alternatives to choose from
question: What does "as well as" mean?

explanation: "Although/Even though" = obwohl. "Although she was tired, she continued working." "Even though it was expensive, he bought it." Introduces a concessive clause.
options: To give a reason or explanation for something that happened
To express a contrast/concession (Although it was raining, we went outside)
To describe the result or consequence of a previous action or situation
To express a time relationship - describing when something happens
question: How do you use "although/even though"?

explanation: "Unless" = es sei denn / wenn nicht. "I'll help you unless you are rude." = "I'll help you if you are NOT rude." Unless + positive condition = negative meaning.
options: wenn / if - introducing a simple condition that may or may not be met
es sei denn dass / wenn nicht (I will come unless it rains = I will come if it doesn't rain)
weil / because - introducing a reason or explanation for something
obwohl / although - introducing a contrast to what was just stated
question: What does "unless" mean?

explanation: Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never): before main verb ("I often read") but after "be" ("She is always tired").
options: Always placed at the very end of the sentence, after the object or complement
Usually before the main verb (I usually wake up at 7) but after be (She is always late)
Always placed at the very beginning of the sentence, before the subject
Only used in questions and never in normal affirmative statements
question: How are adverbs of frequency used?

explanation: "Much" + uncountable: "much water, much time, much money." "Many" + countable (plural): "many books, many people, many hours." In affirmative sentences often: a lot of.
options: There is no difference - both words can be used with any type of noun
Much: for uncountable nouns. Many: for countable nouns (much water, many books)
Much is more polite and formal, many is used in casual everyday speech
Many is used only in questions, while much is used in positive statements
question: What is the difference between "much" and "many"?

explanation: "A few" = ein paar (zahlbar): "a few books, a few friends." "A little" = ein wenig (unzaehlbar): "a little water, a little time." Both are slightly positive (some, not much).
options: There is no difference - both words mean exactly the same thing in all contexts
A few: a small number of (countable). A little: a small amount of (uncountable). Both are positive.
A few is negative and means almost nothing at all is available
A little means absolutely none - that there is zero amount of something
question: What is the difference between "a few" and "a little"?

explanation: Gerund: Verb + -ing als Nomen. "Swimming is my hobby." (Subjekt). "She enjoys reading." (Objekt nach enjoys, like, love, hate, avoid, finish, suggest). After prepositions.
options: Verb + -ed, forming the past tense which then acts as a noun (played is my hobby)
Verb + -ing when the verb acts as a subject or object (Swimming is fun. She loves reading.)
Verb + -s, forming the third person singular used as a noun
Verb + -tion, creating a noun from the verb (information, situation)
question: How do you form the gerund (-ing form used as noun)?

explanation: Verben die Gerund verlangen: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, imagine, miss, practise, consider. "I enjoy swimming." "She avoids eating sugar." "Mind = stoert es dich?"
options: After to, want, would like (I want to swim / I would like to go)
After enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, imagine (I enjoy swimming / She avoids eating sugar)
After will, would, can, must (modals followed by bare infinitive)
After want, need, hope (verbs that take to + infinitive)
question: After which verbs do we usually use a gerund (-ing)?

explanation: "Whereas" = wohingegen, waehrend hingegen. Drueckt einen Kontrast aus. "Some people are morning persons, whereas others prefer evenings." Aehnlich: while, in contrast to.
options: weil / because - introducing a reason or cause for something that happened
wohingegen/waehrend - expressing a contrast (She likes coffee whereas he prefers tea)
obwohl / although - acknowledging something unexpected or surprising
damit / so that - expressing the purpose or goal of an action
question: What does "whereas" mean?

explanation: "So...that" = so...dass. Ergebnis/Folge. "It was so heavy that I couldn't lift it." "She was so tired that she fell asleep immediately."
options: To show a contrast between two different or opposite situations
To show a result (It was so hot that we stayed inside)
To show the reason or cause that explains why something happened
To show a condition that must be met for something to happen
question: How do you use "so...that"?

explanation: Simple Present: 1) Gewohnheiten: "I play football on Sundays." 2) Allgemeine Wahrheiten: "The sun rises in the east." 3) Fahrplaene/Programme: "The train leaves at 8."
options: Actions happening right now at this very moment (I am eating now)
Habits, routines, general truths (I go to school every day. Water boils at 100 degrees.)
Past events that were completed at a specific point in time
Future plans and arrangements that have already been decided
question: What does the Simple Present express?

explanation: 3rd person singular (he/she/it): add -s. Most verbs: play -> plays. Verbs ending in s/x/ch/sh/o: add -es. watch -> watches. go -> goes. Irregular: have -> has.
options: No change - the verb stays exactly the same as the base form (he play)
Add -s or -es (He plays, She watches, It goes)
Add -ing to the base form (He playing, She watching)
Add -ed to create the correct form (He played, She watched)
question: How do you form the Simple Present for he/she/it?

explanation: Simple Present questions: Do (I/you/we/they) + infinitive? Does (he/she/it) + infinitive? "Do you know her?" "Does he live here?" Do NOT add -s after does.
options: Verb + subject + ? (Likes she pizza? Plays he chess?)
Do/Does + subject + infinitive? (Do you like pizza? Does she play chess?)
Did + subject + infinitive? (Did you like pizza? Did she play chess?)
Will + subject + infinitive? (Will you like pizza? Will she play chess?)
question: How do you form Simple Present questions?

explanation: Simple Past: abgeschlossene Handlungen in der Vergangenheit, oft mit Zeitangabe: yesterday, last week, in 1999, ago. "I visited Berlin last summer."
options: Ongoing past actions that were still in progress at a given moment
Completed actions in the past at a specific time (Yesterday, I went to the cinema)
Present habits that repeat regularly in daily life
Future intentions or plans that have already been arranged
question: What is the Simple Past used for?

explanation: "Just" + Present Perfect: etwas ist gerade eben passiert. "He has just called you." "I have just finished my homework." Position: between have/has and the past participle.
options: That something happened a very long time ago, in the distant past
Something happened very recently (She has just arrived)
That an action will happen in the future at a specific time
That an action was repeated many times over a long period
question: What does "just" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Already" = schon/bereits. "I have already done my homework." Position: usually between have/has and past participle, or at end. Used for affirmatives.
options: That something has not yet happened but is expected to happen soon
Something happened sooner than expected (I have already eaten)
That something will definitely happen at some point in the future
That something happened a very long time ago in the distant past
question: What does "already" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Yet" = noch nicht (negativ) / schon (Frage). "I haven't done my homework yet." "Have you called her yet?" Position: end of sentence.
options: That something has already been done sooner than expected
Something expected has NOT happened (I haven't finished yet) OR asking if expected thing happened (Have you eaten yet?)
That something will be done at some future point that has not arrived
That an action was done repeatedly over and over again in the past
question: What does "yet" indicate in the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Ever" = jemals (in Fragen): "Have you ever eaten sushi?" "Never" = nie: "I have never seen snow." Used for life experiences.
options: Specific times in the past when something happened or did not happen
Ever: in your life experience (Have you ever been to Spain?). Never: not in your life.
Future plans and intentions that may or may not be realised
Regular present habits and routines that happen at fixed times
question: What does "ever" and "never" indicate with Present Perfect?

explanation: Past Progressive: was/were + -ing. Beschreibt laufende Handlung zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt in der Vergangenheit. "At 8pm, she was cooking dinner." Often with Simple Past for interruption.
options: A past action that was fully completed at a specific named point in time
An ongoing action at a specific time in the past (I was watching TV when the phone rang)
A habit that was repeated regularly during a period in the past
The Past Perfect - an action completed before another past action
question: What is the Past Progressive (Verlaufsform der Vergangenheit)?

explanation: Past Progressive: was (I/he/she/it) + verb-ing OR were (you/we/they) + verb-ing. "I was sleeping." "They were playing football."
options: had + past participle (had gone, had eaten)
was/were + verb + -ing (I was sleeping / They were playing)
did + verb + -ing (did going, did eating)
used to + infinitive (used to go, used to eat)
question: How do you form the Past Progressive?

explanation: Kombination: "While I was walking home, it started to rain." Past Progressive = laufende Hintergrundhandlung. Simple Past = kurze Unterbrechung.
options: The two tenses are never used together in the same sentence or paragraph
Past Progressive = background/ongoing action; Simple Past = interruption (I was sleeping when the doorbell rang)
Past Progressive always comes after Simple Past to show what happened next
Simple Past describes the ongoing background; Past Progressive the interruption
question: How is the Past Progressive used with the Simple Past?

explanation: Past Perfect: had + Partizip II. Vorvergangenheit. "When I arrived, she had already left." Ereignis 1 (she left) geschah BEVOR Ereignis 2 (I arrived). Signalwoerter: after, before, when, by the time.
options: Another name for the Simple Past - used for ordinary past events
had + past participle - used for actions completed BEFORE another past action (I had eaten before she arrived)
was/were + -ing - an action in progress at a past moment in time
used to + infinitive - a habit that existed in the past but no longer does
question: What is the Past Perfect?

explanation: "By the time she arrived, we had already eaten." Correct: had + past participle (eaten). "By the time" = bis zu dem Zeitpunkt, als... -> Past Perfect usual.
options: I had went to school.
By the time she arrived, we had already eaten.
She had eat the cake.
They had been go home.
question: Which sentence uses the Past Perfect correctly?

explanation: "Will" Future: 1) Spontane Entscheidungen: "I will answer that!" 2) Vorhersagen: "It will be sunny." 3) Versprechen: "I will always love you." 4) Angebote: "I will carry that for you."
options: Fixed plans and arrangements that have already been decided in advance
Spontaneous decisions, predictions, offers, promises (I will help you! It will rain tomorrow.)
Past habits and routines that were regular at a certain time in the past
Current states and conditions that exist at the present moment
question: What does the Future with "will" express?

explanation: "Going to": Plan schon festgelegt: "I am going to visit my aunt on Sunday." Voraussage mit Beweis: "Look! He's going to fall!" Unterschied zu will: Spontan vs. geplant.
options: They are always interchangeable - no difference in meaning exists between them
Going to: for plans already made or evidence-based predictions (Look at those clouds - it's going to rain!)
Going to is always more polite and therefore preferred in formal situations
Will is for fixed plans; going to is for spontaneous decisions made on the spot
question: When do we use "going to" instead of "will"?

explanation: Simple Past Signalwoerter: yesterday, last (week/month/year), ago, in [year], when I was (a child), once, at that time.
options: already, just, ever, never, yet (typical Present Perfect signal words)
yesterday, last week, in 2010, three days ago, when I was young
tomorrow, next week, soon, in the future (future time expressions)
now, at the moment, currently, this very second (present time words)
question: Which time expressions are typically used with the Simple Past?

explanation: Present Perfect Signalwoerter: already, just, yet, ever, never, recently, lately, so far, this (week/month/year), since, for.
options: yesterday, last year, in 2010, three months ago (specific past time points)
already, just, yet, ever, never, recently, so far, this year
tomorrow, next week, next month (future time expressions)
now, at the moment, right now, currently (present time words)
question: Which time expressions are typically used with the Present Perfect?

explanation: "Since" + Zeitpunkt: "since 2010, since Monday, since she left." Used with Present Perfect. "I have known her since we were children." Compare: for + duration.
options: A duration of time with Simple Past (since three years, since a long time)
A point in time with Present Perfect (I have lived here since 2015)
A duration of time with Simple Present (since two hours, since a week)
A specific date with Simple Past (I lived here since 2010 and left in 2015)
question: What is "since" used with?

explanation: "For" + Zeitdauer: "for two hours, for a week, for ten years." With Present Perfect: "I have lived here for five years." Also Simple Past: "She worked there for a year."
options: A specific point in time (for Monday, for 2015, for last Tuesday)
A duration of time (for three years, for a long time, for two weeks)
The beginning of an action (for the first moment, for the start)
A specific date or calendar event (for Christmas, for Saturday)
question: What is "for" used for in time expressions?

explanation: Ertzaehlerische Vergangenheit: Simple Past. "Once upon a time, there was a princess. She lived in a castle. One day, a knight arrived..." Past Progressive fuer Hintergrundbeschreibungen.
options: Simple Present - describing all events as if they are happening right now
Simple Past (and sometimes Past Progressive for background)
Present Perfect - connecting past events to the present moment
Future with will - predicting how the events will unfold
question: What tense do we use to tell a story (narrative tense)?

explanation: Future Progressive: will be + -ing. Zukunftige Handlung in Verlauf zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt. "This time tomorrow, I will be flying to London." Betont den Verlauf.
options: Going to + -ing form (I am going to reading, she is going to working)
Will + be + -ing - used for ongoing future actions (I will be studying all evening)
Was + -ing - describing an action in progress at a past moment
Had + been + -ing - an action in progress before another past action
question: What is the future progressive?

explanation: Fahrplaene/Programme/Spielplaene: Simple Present. "The bus leaves at 9:15." "School starts on Monday." "The film finishes at 10pm." Feste Zeiten im Kalender.
options: Will + infinitive (The train will leave at 8. The film will start at 7.)
Simple Present (The train leaves at 8. The film starts at 7.)
Going to + infinitive (The train is going to leave at 8.)
Past tense - as if the event has already been decided and happened
question: How do we express a scheduled/timetabled future event?

explanation: Simple Past: abgeschlossen, spez. Zeitpunkt. "I saw her yesterday." Present Perfect: Verbindung zur Gegenwart, kein spez. Zeitpunkt. "I have seen her." (Leben, Ergebnis jetzt wichtig).
options: There is no real difference - both tenses describe past events and can be used the same way
Simple Past: finished, specific time in past (yesterday). Present Perfect: connected to now, no specific time / life experience.
Simple Past uses have/has + past participle, not the simple verb form
Present Perfect uses did + infinitive to form questions and negatives
question: What is the main difference between Simple Past and Present Perfect?

explanation: "How long have you + Past Participle?" fragt nach Dauer einer Handlung, die begann und noch laeuft. "How long have you known her?" "I have known her for 3 years." Antwort: for/since.
options: A specific past event that happened once at a definite time in the past
Duration of an action starting in the past and still continuing (How long have you lived here? - For 5 years.)
A future plan or intention that has already been decided and arranged
A completed action that was finished before some other past event
question: What does "How long have you...?" ask about?

explanation: Nach Zeitkonjunktionen (when, before, after, until, as soon as) fuer Zukunft: Simple Present! "When she comes, we will eat." NOT "When she will come".
options: Future with will (I will call you when I will arrive)
Simple Present (I will call you when I arrive - NOT when I will arrive)
Present Perfect (I will call you when I have already arrived)
Past Simple (I called you when I arrived - already happened)
question: What tense do we usually use after time conjunctions like "when, before, after, until" for future?

explanation: Past Perfect mit after/before: zeigt Reihenfolge. "After he had eaten, he went to bed." (essen kam zuerst). "Before I arrived, she had already left." Hatte schon getan.
options: It is never used with these time words - a different tense is always required
To show the sequence of two past events (After she had finished her work, she left)
To describe a future action that will happen after a current one
To describe a past habit that was done regularly at a certain time
question: What is the Past Perfect used for with "after" and "before"?

explanation: Modal verbs + bare infinitive (without to): can swim, must go, should eat. NOT: can swimming, must goes, should to go.
options: Past tense (-ed) (can played, must walked, should talked)
The infinitive without "to" (can swim, must go, should eat)
The -ing form (can swimming, must going, should eating)
The past participle (can swum, must gone, should eaten)
question: Which verb form follows a modal verb?

explanation: "Could" = koennte/konnte. 1) Past ability: "When I was young, I could run fast." 2) Polite request: "Could you help me?" 3) Possibility: "It could rain."
options: can (I can swim when I was five / Can you help me right now?)
could (I could swim when I was five / Could you help me?)
must (I must swim when I was five / Must you help me?)
will (I will swim when I was five / Will you help me please?)
question: How do you say "koennte" (past ability/polite) in English?

explanation: "Must not/Mustn't": verboten. "You mustn't run here." "Don't have to/Doesn't have to": nicht noetig. "You don't have to wear a tie." Completely different meaning!
options: There is no difference at all - must not and don't have to mean exactly the same thing
Must not = forbidden. Don't have to = not necessary (You must not smoke here / You don't have to come)
Must not = not necessary or optional - you can choose whether to do it
Have to is never used in questions - only must can be used to ask questions
question: What is the difference between "must" and "have to" in questions/negatives?

explanation: "Might" = koennte, vielleicht. Schwache Moeglichkeit. "I might go to the party." Less certain than "may". "It might snow tomorrow."
options: Certainty - something will definitely happen without any doubt
Possibility - something may or may not happen (It might rain later - I'm not sure)
Obligation - something that must be done because of a rule or duty
Ability - being physically or mentally capable of doing something
question: What does "might" express?

explanation: "Will" fuer Versprechen und Schwuere: "I will always be there for you." "I will never forget you." Spontane Entscheidung/Versprechen -> will.
options: I am going to love you forever.
I will always be there for you.
I have always loved you.
I was loving you.
question: Which sentence is in the correct future form for a promise?

explanation: "Was/were about to" = wollte gerade... "I was about to call you when you called me." Drueckt aus, dass eine Handlung kurz vor der Ausfuehrung war, als etwas anderes geschah.
options: I had already done something before something else happened
I was just going to do something when something else happened (I was about to leave when the phone rang)
I usually did something at a certain time as part of my routine
I wanted to do something but decided against it in the end
question: What does "I was about to..." mean?

explanation: Present Perfect + since: "She has worked here since 2018." Aktion begann 2018 und dauert bis jetzt an. Auch: Present Perfect Progressive (emphasizes duration): "She has been working here since 2018."
options: Since + Simple Past verb (Since I worked here two years, I know everyone)
Have/has + past participle + since + time point (I have lived here since 2010)
Since + Present Progressive (I am living here since 2010)
Have + been + -ing (also valid for emphasising ongoing action) (I have been living here since 2010)
question: How do you form the Present Perfect with "since" to show duration?

explanation: "Used to": vergangene Zustaende UND Gewohnheiten. "I used to live in Berlin." (Zustand) "Would": nur vergangene Gewohnheiten. "Every Sunday, he would cook a big meal." NOT "I would live in Berlin."
options: Both are used only to describe present habits that happen regularly
Both describe past habits, but "used to" can also describe past states, while "would" is for past actions only
Used to describes plans for the future; would describes completed past actions
Would is used for regular present habits; used to is for one-off past events
question: What does "used to + infinitive" vs "would + infinitive" describe?

explanation: Historisches Praesens: Vergangenes im Praesens erzaehlen um Lebhaftigkeit zu erzeugen. "So I go to the shop, and suddenly I see him!" Gesprochene Sprache, lebhafte Erzaehlung.
options: The exclusive use of present tense in fictional stories and novels
Using present tenses to tell past events more vividly (And then he opens the door and sees her!)
The standard and most common way to tell any kind of story in English
A special type of future tense used to predict upcoming story events
question: What is the "narrative present"?

explanation: Zeitungsschlagzeilen: Simple Present fuer abgeschlossene Ereignisse. "Man Finds Treasure in Garden." "Fire Destroys Hotel." Praesens macht Schlagzeilen kurz und dynamisch.
options: Ongoing actions that are currently happening as the paper is being read
Past events described as present for dramatic effect (Earthquake hits Japan - happened in past)
Future plans and events that are scheduled to happen soon
Conditional or hypothetical situations that may or may not occur
question: What does the "present simple" express in headlines?

explanation: Future Perfect: will + have + Partizip II. "By next year, I will have lived here for 10 years." Handlung wird vor einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt in der Zukunft abgeschlossen sein.
options: Going to + perfect form (I am going to have finished by then)
Will + have + past participle - for actions completed before a future time (By 2025, I will have finished school)
Would + have + past participle - the conditional perfect for unreal situations
Am going to + past participle - a planned action in the near future
question: What is the Future Perfect?

explanation: "Hardly/scarcely/barely...when": kaum...als. Inversion noetig: "Hardly had I arrived when it started raining." = "I had hardly arrived when it started raining."
options: A general time clause describing when two events both happen regularly
As soon as something happened, something else immediately followed (Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang)
A conditional relationship where one event causes the other to happen
A contrast between two events that happened at very different times
question: What does "hardly/scarcely/barely...when/before" express?

explanation: "By the time you read this, I will have already left." Future Perfect fuer Handlung, die BEVOR einem Zeitpunkt in der Zukunft abgeschlossen sein wird.
options: will have left (Future Perfect)
had left (Past Perfect)
have left (Present Perfect)
will leave
question: Which tense is correct in: "By the time you read this, I ___ already ___."?

explanation: be + past participle = Passiv. Simple Present Passiv: "English is spoken worldwide." Simple Past Passiv: "The letter was written." Present Perfect Passiv: "The bridge has been built."
options: Active present - a subject doing something to an object right now
Passive voice (The book is read by many people)
Progressive form - an action in progress at the current moment
Perfect form - an action completed before the current moment
question: What is "to be + past participle" in terms of tense/voice?
